preamble: Solutions to asterisked clues are of a kind and may not be further defined.

clue.text: Triangle functions on point of intimacy

parts.note: cosines are trigonometric functions, worked out from a right-angled triangle
S, south, is a point of the compass

explanation.surface: A maths lesson where triangles somehow get romantic, with functions focused on the point of intimacy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Point' in crosswords is usually a compass point: N, S, E or W.
explanation.definitionFit: Cosiness is a snug, warm closeness between people, which is a near synonym for intimacy.

clue.text: *Party for cathedral functionaries, say

indicators.note: 'say' asks us to speak the phrase and listen to it rather than read its spelling

parts.note: canons are clergy attached to a cathedral, and a treat is a party laid on for them

explanation.surface: A description of a social event put on for the clergy who run a cathedral.
explanation.walkthrough: The preamble says asterisked answers are of a kind: all are London railway termini, so this one has no definition of its own. Cannon Street is a station in the City of London.
explanation.definitionFit: The preamble groups the starred answers as London main-line stations, and Cannon Street is one of those termini.

clue.text: See 1
Temporary structure in the Sun's building

indicators.note: building means constructing, so the letters are put together into a new form

parts.note: every letter of these words is used

explanation.surface: A makeshift building tucked inside the offices of the Sun newspaper.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Building' looks like a noun naming the Sun's office, but it is a verb telling us to construct new letters.
explanation.definitionFit: A Nissen hut is a prefabricated corrugated-iron shelter used in wartime, a classic makeshift building.

clue.text: Poor attenders fell on Jeremy or Simon coming up to the monsoon

parts.note: the first part of Scafell, the Lake District fell; Araucaria lets the word fell stand for what precedes it

indicators.note: in a down entry, coming up means being read from bottom to top, so the name runs backwards

parts.note: Jeremy Brett the actor, or Simon Brett the crime writer
the monsoon is the season of heavy rains

explanation.surface: People who skip things tumble onto a pair of Englishmen just before the rainy season arrives.
explanation.walkthrough: The SCA piece is a loose Araucaria joke: Scafell is the famous fell, so 'fell on' asks what sits in front of fell. Brett is the surname shared by both named men.
explanation.definitionFit: Scatterbrains are forgetful, disorganised people, who pay poor attention in the sense of attending badly to things.

clue.text: Enlarge Fawkes's purpose?

definitions.meaning: first meaning: to make a photograph bigger
second meaning: Guy Fawkes plotted in 1605 to destroy Parliament with gunpowder

explanation.walkthrough: Guy Fawkes, of the Gunpowder Plot, is remembered in Britain every 5 November with bonfires and fireworks. The question mark flags the playful second sense.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrasal verb serves both for magnifying a picture and for destroying something with explosives.

clue.text: House hosting game in 14

definitions.meaning: first meaning: the upper chamber of the British Parliament, whose members are peers

definitions.note: describes the ground, Lord's, which hosts the game
definitions.meaning: second meaning: the London cricket ground in St John's Wood; 14-down's wordplay begins with the game of cricket

explanation.walkthrough: 14-down's wordplay starts with 'Game heard', which is cricket, so the game here is cricket. Lord's in St John's Wood is the most famous cricket ground in England.
explanation.definitionFit: The word names both the upper parliamentary chamber and the historic London venue staging Test cricket.

clue.text: *Crapper's invention (according to the myth)

parts.note: surface reading: the flushing lavatory, which legend credits to the plumber Thomas Crapper; setter's reading: the invention is a lavatory flushed with liquid, a phrase that names a London station

explanation.walkthrough: Thomas Crapper was a Victorian plumber popularly but wrongly said to have invented the flush toilet; loo is British slang for toilet. The preamble supplies the category: London termini.
explanation.definitionFit: The preamble groups starred answers as London stations, and Waterloo is the busiest terminus south of the Thames.

clue.text: Heaven is in the display

indicators.note: one thing being in another means it sits inside it

parts.note: a parade is a public display or show
taken as written

explanation.surface: A statement that bliss is found in a spectacle or show.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Is' looks like the verb of the sentence but is the letters to be inserted.
explanation.definitionFit: Paradise is the blissful afterlife of the righteous, a direct synonym for heaven.

clue.text: As seductive woman returned, so did her ring

definitions.note: describes the character through her ring, which came back to her

indicators.note: to return is to go back the way one came, so the letters run backwards

parts.note: taken as written
a siren is a dangerously alluring woman, after the singers of Greek myth

explanation.surface: A tale of a temptress coming back, with her ring coming back too.
explanation.walkthrough: In The Merchant of Venice, Nerissa gives Gratiano a ring he must keep; he gives it away, and she tricks him into returning it to her.
explanation.definitionFit: Shakespeare's Nerissa, Portia's maid, is the woman whose ring famously comes back to her at the play's end.

clue.text: He keeps a dog and a Manx cat on river

definitions.note: a museum keeper is one who keeps the collection; the noun phrase stands for the person

parts.note: a cur is a mongrel dog

indicators.note: a Manx cat has no tail, so the word for cat loses its last letter

parts.note: a tom is a male cat

explanation.surface: A man who owns a dog and a tailless Isle of Man cat lives by a river.
explanation.walkthrough: Manx cats are famously tailless, so 'Manx cat' is TOM without its tail, TO. 'He keeps' is the definition: a keeper of a museum or gallery.
explanation.definitionFit: A museum keeper is in charge of its collections, which is exactly the job title of this official.

clue.text: Most of 9 goods between birds — that's the best thing of all

indicators.note: between means the other letters sit inside, splitting the two bird names

parts.note: the crow and the lory (a parrot) are two birds

indicators.note: most of means the last letter of the number word is dropped

parts.note: the number nine written as a word
G is short for good, and goods gives two of them

explanation.surface: Most of nine goods placed between two birds is said to be the finest thing.
explanation.walkthrough: The 9 here is the plain number, not a cross-reference to 9 across; and 'goods' is a plural of the abbreviation for good, so it supplies the letter twice. A lory is a small parrot.
explanation.definitionFit: A crowning glory is an idiom for the supreme achievement or most impressive feature.

clue.text: Honours drug to make one fat

parts.note: OBEs, Orders of the British Empire, are British honours
E is slang for the drug ecstasy

explanation.surface: A warning that some honours-list medicine will cause weight gain.
explanation.walkthrough: The OBE is an award in the British honours system, given at royal investitures.
explanation.definitionFit: Obese means extremely overweight, a stronger synonym for fat.

clue.text: Bagged journalist after time with alarm clock?

parts.note: T is the abbreviation for time
an alarm clock rouses sleepers, so it is a rouser
ED, editor, is the usual crossword journalist

explanation.surface: A reporter caught out after a while by a ringing alarm clock.
explanation.walkthrough: 'After' puts the journalist last. To trouser is British slang for pocketing money, often dubiously.
explanation.definitionFit: To trouser something is to pocket it, and bagged likewise means took or grabbed for oneself.

clue.text: * Church with a set of bells to go over

parts.note: CH is the abbreviation for church
a ring is a full set of church bells for change-ringing
to cross is to go over

explanation.surface: A church whose bells must be checked over or passed across.
explanation.walkthrough: The preamble's category is London termini, so there is no definition here. Charing Cross is a station beside Trafalgar Square.
explanation.definitionFit: The starred answers share the preamble's theme of London railway termini, and Charing Cross is one.

clue.text: Game heard, maybe hard, in north Wales

indicators.note: heard asks for what is spoken and listened to, not what is spelt

parts.note: the bat-and-ball game, said with hard C sounds and a Welsh ending

explanation.surface: A sport played tough somewhere in the north of Wales.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Maybe hard' admits the match is only rough: the double C in the Welsh name is said as a hard K. Criccieth is a small seaside town on the Llŷn peninsula.
explanation.definitionFit: Criccieth is a castle town on Cardigan Bay, a place situated in north Wales.

clue.text: Is one of those in 13 a queen, …

parts.note: taken as written
13-across contains a ring, a set of bells, so one of them is a bell
taken as written

explanation.surface: Asking whether one of a church's bells could be royalty.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue runs on into 16-down with dots, so the next answer is 'another' queen. Isabella of Castile sponsored Columbus.
explanation.definitionFit: Several queens bore the name Isabella, most famously the Spanish monarch who ruled Castile with Ferdinand.

clue.text: *… another 7 ac wandering round hill?

definitions.note: following on from 15, another of the London stations and another queen; as an asterisked clue it needs no fuller definition

indicators.note: the scrambled letters go round the hill, enclosing it on either side
letters that go wandering stray from their places, so the Roman seven and the letters ac are rearranged

parts.note: seven in Roman numerals is VII, taken together with the letters ac as one batch of fodder
a tor is a rocky hill, especially on Dartmoor

explanation.surface: Continuing from the previous clue, it asks whether another station near Waterloo is a wanderer around a hill.
explanation.walkthrough: '7' looks like a cross-reference to WATERLOO at 7, but here it is just the Roman numeral VII. VII with AC, 'wandering', gives VICIA, which goes 'round' TOR. The preamble lets asterisked answers, all London termini, go undefined; 'another' follows on from Queen ISABELLA at 15.
explanation.definitionFit: Victoria is a London mainline terminus like the other starred answers, and also a queen, so it is another of the kind.

clue.text: Umbrian master in crafts as in order

indicators.note: putting things in order means arranging them afresh

parts.note: every letter of these words is used

explanation.surface: An Italian painter skilled in crafts, working in sequence.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Umbrian master' suggests a Renaissance painter such as Perugino; 'order' hints at the Franciscan religious order he founded.
explanation.definitionFit: Francis of Assisi, from Umbria, founded and led the Franciscan friars, so he was master of an order.

clue.text: *Left like Aberdeen with game

parts.note: L is the abbreviation for left
Aberdeen stands on the river Don, so it is on Don
a card game

explanation.surface: Someone abandoned in a Scottish city with a sport to play.
explanation.walkthrough: Aberdeen sits at the mouths of the Dee and the Don; describing it as on Don gives the middle piece. The preamble covers the definition: London termini.
explanation.definitionFit: London Bridge is one of the capital's main-line termini, matching the preamble's shared category.

clue.text: See 18
Queen gets in — "in" as in 14's game — with ram

definitions.note: a phrase that the answer completes, as in battering ram

indicators.note: getting in means entering, so one piece is placed inside another

parts.note: in cricket the side that is in is batting
ER, Elizabeth Regina, is the crossword queen

explanation.surface: A queen arriving at a cricket match and joining in with a male sheep.
explanation.walkthrough: 14's game is cricket, where 'in' means having a turn at batting. The definition is a fill-in: the answer goes with ram.
explanation.definitionFit: A battering ram is a heavy beam for breaking down gates, so the word is what goes with ram.

clue.text: English Guardian's going to Surrey town

parts.note: E is the abbreviation for English
a newspaper speaks of itself as we, so the paper is going to means we will, shortened

explanation.surface: An English newspaper reporter heading off to a town in Surrey.
explanation.walkthrough: Surrey is a county just south-west of London. Editorials use 'we', and 'we will' contracts with an apostrophe that the grid ignores.
explanation.definitionFit: Ewell is a small town near Epsom in the county of Surrey, so it fits the geographical description.

clue.text: They sing in church or outside one

parts.note: CH is the abbreviation for church

indicators.note: being outside something means wrapping around it

parts.note: taken as written
I is the Roman numeral one

explanation.surface: Singers who perform either inside a church or out in the churchyard.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Outside' seems to describe where the singers stand, but it tells us to wrap one piece around another.
explanation.definitionFit: A choir is a group of singers, so it is a collective noun that sings.

clue.text: Generosity sees glass re-turned

indicators.note: something turned is moved about out of its original position

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written, split off by the hyphen

explanation.surface: A kindly gesture is to give a drinking glass back to its owner.
explanation.walkthrough: The hyphen splits the word, leaving RE as letters to mix in and 'turned' as the instruction; read whole it suggests a reversal.
explanation.definitionFit: Largess is generous giving of money or gifts, a near synonym for generosity.

clue.text: Exaggerated love before composer died

parts.note: love is zero in tennis, which looks like O
Giuseppe Verdi, the Italian opera composer
D is the abbreviation for died

explanation.surface: A melodramatic summary of an opera: overblown passion before the composer's death.
explanation.walkthrough: Love meaning nil comes from tennis scoring.
explanation.definitionFit: To overdo something is to carry it too far, so overdid matches the past-tense sense of exaggerated.

clue.text: Can nearly work this land?

definitions.note: describes land that can be worked; the answer is an adjective

indicators.note: nearly means not quite all, so the first word stops one letter short

parts.note: can means are able; the first of the two words then loses its final letter

explanation.surface: A farmer wondering whether a field is fit for cultivation.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Can' is a verb that expands to two words, the first of which is cut short.
explanation.definitionFit: Arable land is suitable for ploughing and growing crops, the kind of soil a farmer can work.

clue.text: Legendary Welsh king has no right to join the Church of England, as it happens

indicators.note: to have none of something means it is taken away

parts.note: Brychan, the legendary king of Brycheiniog in Wales, less one letter
R is the abbreviation for right, the letter removed
CE is the abbreviation for the Church of England

explanation.surface: An ancient Welsh ruler, lacking any rights, enrolling in the Anglican church as luck would have it.
explanation.walkthrough: Brychan was a fifth-century king who gave his name to Brecknock, the old county around Brecon.
explanation.definitionFit: By chance means accidentally or as it turns out, an idiom matching as it happens.
